acceptedAnswer.text: Tooth contouring is often well tolerated. Only a very small amount of enamel is removed, and enamel itself contains no nerve endings. Many patients do not require anaesthetic. Some individuals with naturally thinner enamel or existing sensitivity may notice mild discomfort, so your dentist will assess your enamel thickness beforehand and discuss any concerns with you during the consultation.

mainEntity.name: How long does composite bonding last?

acceptedAnswer.text: Composite bonding typically lasts between three and seven years, though this varies significantly between individuals depending on lifestyle habits, oral hygiene, diet, and whether bruxism (teeth grinding) is a factor. The material can chip, stain, or wear over time. Regular dental check-ups allow the dentist to monitor the condition of the bonding and carry out minor repairs or polishing as needed. Longevity cannot be guaranteed.

mainEntity.name: Will my teeth look obviously treated after composite bonding and contouring?

acceptedAnswer.text: When carried out by an experienced dentist, the goal of combining composite bonding with tooth contouring is to achieve a refined, natural result. The treatment is designed for subtlety. Most patients find that others notice their smile looks better without being able to identify a specific change. The outcome depends on the skill of the clinician, the materials used, and the suitability of the treatment for your individual dental structure.

mainEntity.name: Can I have composite bonding if I have existing fillings?

acceptedAnswer.text: In many cases, yes — but this depends on the location and condition of existing restorations. Composite resin bonds differently to filling materials than it does to natural enamel. Your dentist will examine your existing dental work during the consultation to determine whether composite bonding can be applied effectively and how it will integrate with the surrounding teeth and restorations.

mainEntity.name: Is composite bonding a good alternative to veneers?

acceptedAnswer.text: Composite bonding and porcelain veneers both address cosmetic concerns, but they are different treatments suited to different circumstances. Composite bonding is generally less invasive, more affordable, and reversible, but may not last as long or achieve the same degree of colour stability as porcelain. Veneers typically require more enamel preparation but offer greater durability and stain resistance. Your dentist can help you understand which option aligns best with your clinical situation and aesthetic goals. You can find out more about cosmetic dentistry options at Smile Dentist to begin exploring your choices.

mainEntity.name: Is there any recovery time after these treatments?

acceptedAnswer.text: There is typically no recovery time required following composite bonding or tooth contouring. Most patients return to normal activities immediately. You may be advised to avoid very hot or cold foods and drinks for a short period following bonding, and to be cautious with staining foods in the initial days. If you experience any unexpected sensitivity or discomfort after treatment, it is always worth contacting your dental practice for guidance.
